title: Book 8 — Urania, Chapter 68
paragraphs: So as Mardonius went round questioning them, beginning with the king of Sidon, the others all gave the same opinion, advising him to fight at sea — but Artemisia spoke these words: “Tell the king, I pray you, Mardonius, that I — who have proven myself not the worst in the sea-fights near Euboea, having performed deeds not inferior to those of others — speak to him thus: ‘Master, it is right that I set forth the opinion I really hold, and say what I happen to think best for your cause: and this I say — spare your ships, and do not make a sea-fight. For the men are stronger than your men at sea by as much as men are stronger than women. And why must you run the risk of a sea-battle? Do you not have Athens in your possession — for which you marched out — and the rest of Greece as well? No one stands in your way to resist; those who did stand against you have come off as they deserved. Now I will declare how I think your adversaries' affairs will turn out. If you do not hurry to make a sea-fight, but keep your ships here by the land — either remaining here yourself or even advancing toward the Peloponnese — what you have come to do, O master, will easily be accomplished. For the Greeks cannot hold out against you for long; you will soon scatter them, and they will flee to their various cities, since (as I am told) they have no provisions with them on this island, nor is it likely that, if you march your land-army against the Peloponnese, those of them who came from there will remain still — for they will have no concern to fight a battle in defense of Athens. But if you hurry to fight at once, I fear that damage to the fleet may ruin the land-army as well. Moreover, O king, consider this too: servants of good men tend to become bad, while those of bad men become good. You, the best of all men, have bad servants — those reckoned among your allies: Egyptians, Cyprians, Cilicians, Pamphylians, who are of no use to you.'”
